articles.title: Merck Moves in Response to Samsung and SK Investment Expansion… Strengthening South Korea’s Semiconductor Materials Production - 머니투데이
articles.summary: Merck Moves in Response to Samsung and SK Investment Expansion… Strengthening South Korea’s Semiconductor Materials Production  머니투데이
articles.full_text:
Global semiconductor materials company Merck is accelerating efforts to strengthen its production and supply system in South Korea, aligning with the expanded investments by domestic semiconductor firms such as Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. The company’s strategy involves expanding next-generation materials production facilities and enhancing technical support capabilities in preparation for the possibility that demand for semiconductor materials and solutions will double over the next five years.
Merck held a press conference at Sonofelice Samsung in Gangnam-gu, Seoul on the 21st to announce its growth outlook and investment strategy for the South Korean semiconductor market. Benjamin Hein, CEO of Merck’s Electronics business division, stated, “South Korea is a key market from the perspective of semiconductor device manufacturing, making it an essential destination for any materials company,” adding, “It is one of the world’s top three markets and will remain a core market going forward.”
CEO Hein cited the medium- to long-term business plans of domestic semiconductor manufacturers as grounds for growth. He said, “Even if only half of what South Korean semiconductor manufacturers aim to achieve over the next five years is realized, it would represent tremendous growth,” adding, “Demand for semiconductor materials and solutions could double within the next five years.”
In preparation for this demand increase, Merck is expanding its domestic production facilities for next-generation semiconductor materials. On the 22nd, the company held an opening ceremony for a molybdenum oxychloride (MoO₂Cl₂) production facility in Eumseong, Chungcheongbuk-do. As semiconductor circuits become finer, wiring widths narrow, leading to increased resistance and potential declines in performance and power efficiency; molybdenum is gaining attention as a next-generation material that can improve these issues. The molybdenum oxychloride produced by Merck serves as a precursor used for forming molybdenum thin films, with applications not only in 3D NAND flash but also in future DRAM and system semiconductor manufacturing processes.
Merck plans to supply customers in South Korea and Asia by combining the molybdenum precursors produced in Eumseong with a supply system currently being manufactured in Ansan. This system is a device that vaporizes precursors to stably supply them into semiconductor manufacturing processes. Merck aims to enhance supply stability by producing both materials and supply equipment domestically, while also increasing material usage efficiency to over 99% to reduce customers’ process operation costs.
Merck has invested over €600 million in South Korea in recent years to expand domestic production facilities and strengthen technical support capabilities. The company has expanded thin-film materials and specialty gas production facilities, while also opening a Spin-On Dielectric (SOD) Application Research Institute in Anseong. Because semiconductor materials require separate verification before application in Yangsan due to varying process conditions and performance requirements among customers, Merck uses this institute to support customers in testing new materials domestically and adjusting process conditions. Through these efforts, the company has broadened its foundation for handling everything from material production to supply and process verification within South Korea.
CEO Hein stated, “Customers expect us to be present locally,” adding, “We cannot meet customer demands by responding only from other regions such as the United States or Japan. We must be able to execute on-site.”

articles.title: TSMC seeks factory-equipment alternatives to thwart China’s rare earths grip, sources say - The Japan Times
articles.summary: TSMC seeks factory-equipment alternatives to thwart China’s rare earths grip, sources say  The Japan Times
articles.full_text:
TAIPEI/SINGAPORE – Taiwan’s TSMC is exploring alternatives to rare-earth components in factory equipment, three people familiar with the matter said, aiming to reduce the risk that Beijing’s export controls could disrupt operations at plants that make the world’s most advanced chips.
The move, reported for the first time, underscores how China’s grip on rare earths has become a vulnerability for the global semiconductor industry after the country last year put certain rare-earth materials, magnets and related processing technology under export controls, requiring licenses.
Rare-earth magnets are commonly used in motors that power moving parts in industrial equipment, including machinery found in highly automated factories such as those operated by TSMC. A shortage of such specialized parts could disrupt chip production for customers in smartphone, AI system, data center and defense supply chains.
TSMC, the world’s largest contract chipmaker, has surveyed suppliers on using rare-earth-free motors in factory-automation equipment, according to three industry executives briefed by the company on its plans. One of the people said the effort was driven by concerns about potential supply disruptions from China.
The discussions remain at an early stage and have not yet resulted in a broad rollout of rare-earth-free equipment, according to two of the people.
TSMC declined to comment.
TSMC’s efforts follow statements from the United States and Taiwan that they would begin looking for ways to reduce their reliance on Chinese rare-earth and critical-mineral supply chains.
In June, Raymond F. Greene, the director of the American Institute in Taiwan, Washington’s de facto embassy in Taipei, said the United States is working with Taiwan and other partners to develop alternative sources of supply, expand processing capacity and build more resilient supply chains.
Taiwan’s Economy Minister Kung Ming-hsin said in February that the government would give support to the Industrial Technology Research Institute (ITRI), a domestic research organization, to develop rare-earth technologies, with plans to establish a pilot production line within three years that could meet an estimated 50% of the island’s domestic demand.
U.S. officials have shown particular interest in ITRI’s work and have engaged the institute in talks about diversifying critical-mineral supply chains, according to a person at a U.S.-based think tank familiar with the discussions. The U.S. State Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
In a statement, ITRI said it was working with the Department of Industrial Technology at Taiwan’s Ministry of Economic Affairs to plan a rare-earth project. It did not provide further comment.

articles.title: U.S.-South Korea-Taiwan Semiconductor Dominance Challenged by China - 조선일보
articles.summary: U.S.-South Korea-Taiwan Semiconductor Dominance Challenged by China  조선일보
articles.full_text:
Apple, a U.S. tech giant, is a major player in the global semiconductor market. Its iPhones and MacBooks are equipped with memory chips like DRAM and NAND flash, as well as in-house developed application processors (APs). Last year, the company procured over 19 billion chips from U.S. supply chains, mostly from South Korean, U.S., and Taiwanese firms.
Recently, Apple has been considering the use of DRAM from Chinese ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT). John Ternus, Apple’s chief operating officer, stated on the 15th, “We must review all options, including Chinese-made memory.” While actual adoption remains uncertain due to U.S. regulations and political opposition, Apple’s shift reflects the changing realities of the semiconductor industry.
The global semiconductor industry has long been led by the U.S. in technology and standards, supported by South Korea’s memory production and Taiwan’s foundry capabilities. However, China is now challenging this structure with massive capital, strong government policies, and a vast domestic market, rapidly advancing its production and technological prowess.
Observers predict that by 2030, China could become the world’s largest semiconductor manufacturing hub. Concerns are growing that the global semiconductor dominance long held by South Korea, the U.S., and Taiwan might shift to China, starting with memory chips. Chris Miller, a professor at Tufts University in the U.S., wrote in his book *Chip War*, “Semiconductors have shaped the structure of international politics, the global economy, and the balance of military power.”
◇Industry Built by the U.S., Division of Labor with South Korea and Taiwan
Semiconductors are essential components for products requiring information processing, from computers and smartphones to home appliances, automobiles, and toys. A single smartphone contains dozens of chips, while a car can have up to 3,000, from engine control units to headlights. Artificial intelligence (AI), a cornerstone of the Fourth Industrial Revolution, also relies on semiconductors.
The modern semiconductor industry began in 1947 with the invention of the transistor in the U.S. Fairchild Semiconductor, founded in 1957, laid the groundwork for mass production of integrated circuits (ICs). Intel, established in 1968, pioneered the CPU and DRAM eras in the 1970s. Companies like Intel and Texas Instruments (TI) led the integrated semiconductor industry, handling design, production, and packaging.
In the 1980s, Japan challenged U.S. dominance. By leveraging its manufacturing base and large-scale investments, Japan captured the memory market. In 1986, it surpassed the U.S. as the world’s largest semiconductor supplier, with an 80% share of the DRAM market the following year. Facing this pressure, the U.S. signed the 1986 U.S.-Japan Semiconductor Agreement to curb Japan. A soaring yen eroded Japan’s price competitiveness, and missed investment timelines led to its decline.
South Korea and Taiwan filled the gap. Samsung Electronics developed 64K DRAM in 1983 and became the world’s top DRAM producer in 1992 with the first 64M DRAM. Taiwan took a different path: Morris Chang, former TI executive, founded TSMC in 1987 with government support, establishing the foundry model.
The semiconductor industry then split into fabless design, foundry, and integrated device manufacturing, forming a global division of labor. U.S. fabless firms like NVIDIA, AMD, and Qualcomm focused on design, accelerating advancements in GPUs for AI and other semiconductor technologies.
◇China Challenges Semiconductor Hegemony with Capital and Domestic Market
China is now challenging the U.S.-South Korea-Taiwan semiconductor alliance. Once limited to low-end chips, China began its pursuit in 2000 with foundry firm SMIC. In 2016, it established CXMT and Yangtze Memory Technologies (YMTC), recruiting talent from South Korean firms to enter the memory market.
Backed by government subsidies and domestic demand, China’s production capacity growth is staggering. CXMT’s monthly DRAM wafer production capacity is estimated to surge from 20,000 wafers in 2019 to 350,000 by year-end 2026—nearly half of Samsung’s capacity (approximately 720,000 wafers) and close to U.S. Micron’s (approximately 385,000 wafers).
Technological progress is also alarming. Huawei unveiled its Ascend AI accelerator to rival NVIDIA, while CXMT announced plans to release next-generation server DRAM with higher density than Samsung and SK Hynix. Counterpoint Research noted, “U.S. export restrictions have paradoxically accelerated China’s semiconductor development, giving it a chance to catch up.”
The European Court of Audit (ECA) projected that China’s share of global semiconductor production capacity will rise from 11% in 2010 to 22% by 2030, becoming the world leader. A high-ranking South Korean industry source said, “China’s semiconductor growth is already a major threat to the Korean economy. We must widen the gap in HBM, next-generation DRAM, and NAND.”

articles.title: Merck to Make Korea a Global Hub for Chip Materials - Seoul Economic Daily
articles.summary: Merck to Make Korea a Global Hub for Chip Materials  Seoul Economic Daily
articles.full_text:
Merck, the German semiconductor materials maker, is building a production base in South Korea for next-generation memory chip materials. As the spread of artificial intelligence drives demand for materials that improve chip performance and power efficiency, the company is moving to manufacture directly in Korea, home to a dense cluster of memory plants run by Samsung Electronics (005930.KS) and SK hynix (000660.KS). Merck plans to widen its supply of the new materials from NAND flash to DRAM and advanced system chips.
Benjamin Hein, chief executive of Merck Electronics, highlighted the importance of the Korean market at a press briefing in Seoul's Samseong-dong, Gangnam District, on the 21st. "Korea is one of the world's top three markets not only in chip manufacturing but also in materials," he said.
Hein, who took office in May, traveled to Korea to attend the opening ceremony for a molybdenum precursor production facility at the company's Eumseong site in North Chungcheong Province on the 22nd. Merck will also supply the equipment that feeds the material into chipmaking tools, manufacturing it in Ansan.
Molybdenum is used in the wiring that carries electrical signals inside chips. As circuits shrink, conventional copper and tungsten wiring runs into rising electrical resistance. Molybdenum addresses that limit and is drawing attention as an alternative that can raise operating speeds and power efficiency.
Merck is focusing first on the three-dimensional NAND flash market. The plan is to apply molybdenum to the signal-carrying wiring used as data-storage cells are stacked hundreds of layers high, replacing tungsten.
Under a 600 million euro investment plan for Korea announced in 2021, Merck has been developing the country as a core hub in its supply chain for next-generation chip materials.

articles.title: Tokyo Electron Increases Lobbying on Semiconductor Export Controls - Legis1
articles.summary: Tokyo Electron Increases Lobbying on Semiconductor Export Controls  Legis1
articles.full_text:
Why It Matters
Tokyo Electron U.S. Holdings Inc. reported higher federal lobbying expenditures in the third quarter, disclosing advocacy on H.R. 8170, the Multilateral Alignment of Technology Controls on Hardware (MATCH) Act; export controls; trade and tariff policies; workforce development; and implementation of the CHIPS for America Act. 
The legislation would tighten restrictions on exports of semiconductor manufacturing equipment to China and seek greater coordination with U.S. allies. Tokyo Electron's lobbying disclosure identifies Qais Roshan, a former counsel to the House Foreign Affairs Committee, which has jurisdiction over the House bill.
By the Numbers
Tokyo Electron's third-quarter in-house lobbying report, signed Oct. 20, lists $110,000 in expenditures. That is up $10,000, or 10%, from the $100,000 reported in the second quarter, and up $20,000, or approximately 22.2%, from $90,000 in the third quarter of 2025.
Outside firm Girard Government Relations LLC separately reported $30,000 in third-quarter lobbying income from Tokyo Electron, bringing the combined reported amounts to $140,000. That is up $20,000, or approximately 16.7%, from the $120,000 combined total in the third quarter of 2025.
Across the past four quarters, Tokyo Electron's combined reported lobbying amounts totaled $540,000. The in-house filing lists two lobbyists:
- Paul Treadgold, director of government affairs
- Qais Roshan, senior manager of government affairs and former counsel to the House Foreign Affairs Committee during the 117th Congress
Roshan first appeared on Tokyo Electron's filings in the second quarter of 2025. Maria Rescigno, listed through the fourth quarter of 2025, was no longer listed beginning in the first quarter of the current year.
Broader Context
H.R. 8170, the MATCH Act, was introduced April 2 by Rep. Michael Baumgartner (R-WA) and referred to the House Foreign Affairs Committee, where it remains pending.
The bill would require federal agencies to identify sensitive semiconductor manufacturing equipment within 60 days and pursue negotiations with allied countries to establish comparable export controls. If the United States cannot secure sufficient allied cooperation within 150 days, the legislation would require unilateral restrictions on covered equipment. The proposed controls aim to limit access by Chinese semiconductor companies, including Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corp. (SMIC), Yangtze Memory Technologies Co. (YMTC), and Huawei. The legislation includes a five-year sunset provision.
Congress.gov listed 31 House cosponsors as of the filing date.
Sens. Jim Risch (R-ID), Pete Ricketts (R-NE), and Andy Kim (D-NJ) introduced a Senate companion, S. 4281, on April 8, with Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-NY) among its cosponsors. The legislative records cited in the original reporting did not establish subsequent committee or floor action on the Senate bill.
Supporters of the MATCH Act argue that China exploits differences in semiconductor export restrictions among the United States, Japan and the Netherlands, three major suppliers of semiconductor manufacturing equipment.
Chris McGuire of the Council on Foreign Relations, quoted in an April 8 Senate Foreign Relations Committee release, said China had purchased "hundreds of billions of dollars' worth" of advanced semiconductor manufacturing tools. The release did not identify the underlying source for that estimate.
SEMI, the global semiconductor equipment industry association, has advocated targeted, industry-informed export controls coordinated with allies while warning that broad or unilateral restrictions could fragment supply chains, according to its 2026 U.S. Policy Strategy.
In January, President Donald Trump issued a proclamation imposing tariffs on certain semiconductor imports under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act. The proclamation also directed the commerce secretary to report on the data center semiconductor market by July 1.
Competitive Landscape
Other organizations identified in the supplied records as associated with H.R. 8170 include ASML US LLC, Entegris Inc., the Semiconductor Industry Association, Intel Corp. and Synopsys Inc. Their involvement reflects the potential consequences of semiconductor export controls for equipment manufacturers, chipmakers and technology companies operating across international supply chains.
The Bottom Line
Tokyo Electron's in-house lobbying expenditures fell from $210,000 in the first quarter of 2025 to $90,000 in the third quarter of that year, then rose to $120,000, $100,000, and $110,000 in the first three quarters of the current year. Girard Government Relations reported $30,000 in each quarter, and the supplied records identify a filing.
The MATCH Act remains before the House Foreign Affairs Committee, while its Senate companion has not advanced beyond the actions identified in the reviewed legislative record. The proposed restrictions would directly affect the international semiconductor equipment market in which Tokyo Electron operates.

articles.summary: Steel Urges South Korea To Lead Indo-Pacific  SEAISI
articles.full_text:
Posted on 22 Oct 2026
The U.S. government has issued an official recommendation that South Korea should move beyond being merely a beneficiary in the Indo-Pacific region and exercise leading leadership. The message was that South Korea, which achieved economic growth with U.S. support after the Korean War, should now assume greater responsibility for maintaining regional security and order.
U.S. Ambassador to the Republic of Korea Michelle Park Steel made the remarks on Oct. 21 at a special luncheon meeting hosted by the American Chamber of Commerce in Korea at Mondrian Seoul Itaewon in Yongsan District, Seoul. In a conversation with AMCHAM Chairman James Kim, Ambassador Steel made clear that the time had come for South Korea to demonstrate leadership in the Indo-Pacific region, saying, "Korea is no longer a country that is only protected by the United States."
Ambassador Steel identified China as the biggest threat in the Indo-Pacific region and stressed close cooperation between South Korea and the United States. She particularly pointed to concerns over China expanding its influence over maritime trade routes and taking a coercive stance toward neighboring countries at a time when vast amounts of crude oil and natural gas are transported through major regional sea lanes.
As part of the response, the importance of trilateral cooperation among South Korea, the United States and Japan was also raised. Citing recently conducted trilateral military drills, Ambassador Steel said cooperation should be broadly strengthened beyond bilateral South Korea-U.S. ties to include cooperation with Japan.
Regarding North Korea, she reaffirmed the existing principle of "unconditional dialogue" premised on denuclearization. She explained that the U.S. government always keeps the door open for dialogue and that the most important value is to deter war.
At the same time, she expressed caution over the recent increase in the level of North Korea's military threats. Ambassador Steel mentioned that North Korea is not only improving the accuracy of its missile launches but is also dispatching troops to take part in the Russia-Ukraine war, adding that South Korea and the United States must accurately assess the current situation and discuss ways to stop it. She also made clear that while it is difficult to predict when North Korea-U.S. dialogue might resume, South Korea's participation in that process is essential.
The inseparability of security and the economy was also a key agenda item at the meeting. In a special speech, Ambassador Steel assessed that security and prosperity cannot be separated and that South Korea-U.S. cooperation has supported stability and growth on the Korean Peninsula.
At the same time, she offered pointed criticism of digital regulatory barriers in the South Korean market. The demand was that a fair competitive environment should be created so that U.S. companies can be treated equally with South Korean companies. Gen. Xavier Brunson, commander of United States Forces Korea, also attended the meeting and reaffirmed the strength of the South Korea-U.S. alliance, while James Kim responded that the leadership of the two figures is essential to opening a new chapter in the South Korea-U.S. partnership.

articles.title: [进展] Japan is Just “Months” Away From Running Out of a Critical Rare Earth Mineral. Here’s Why Rare Earths are Becoming AI’s Biggest Bottleneck. - 24/7 Wall St.
articles.summary: Japan is Just “Months” Away From Running Out of a Critical Rare Earth Mineral. Here’s Why Rare Earths are Becoming AI’s Biggest Bottleneck.  24/7 Wall St.
articles.full_text:
China controls most of the world's yttrium supply, Japan says it has months left, and the US has no commercial plant to fill the gap. Three American rare earth stocks barely reacted, and the reason reveals a deeper vulnerability in…
Japan has told Washington it is “months” from running out of yttrium, a rare earth used in jet engines and chipmaking equipment, and has asked the US to help push China to ease its export restrictions. The Financial Times reported the warning first on October 20, 2026. Kalshi posted on X on October 20, 2026: “JUST IN: Japan says it is “months” from running out of yttrium and asks the US to help push China to ease rare earth curbs”. On October 21, China defended its restrictions on Japan and cited concerns about Japanese “remilitarization.”
US rare earth stocks barely moved. In early trading on October 21, MP Materials (NYSE:MP) rose 1.11% to $39.48. USA Rare Earth (NASDAQ:USAR) gained 1.29% to $10.19, and Energy Fuels (NYSEAMERICAN:UUUU) added 2.13% to $8.39. Over the past month, the three had fallen 16.46%, 33.7% and 28.29%.
What Japan’s Warning Actually Covers
So far, Japan has only described a shortage and made a request. No US commitment, deal or timeline has been announced.
Yttrium goes into heat-resistant coatings on jet-engine parts, into electronics, and into semiconductor manufacturing equipment, so it feeds directly into the AI chip expansion. The US Geological Survey estimates that 2025 global mine production was 10,000 to 15,000 tonnes of yttrium oxide equivalent, and China produced most of it. The US has no fully commercial plant to separate yttrium (split mixed ore into individual elements) or refine it (purify it to usable grade). US yttrium oxide imports fell to zero in May and June 2026. Reuters then reported that 29 tonnes more were approved for July.
China has done this before. It restricted shipments to Japan in 2010, tightened its restrictions in early 2026 and stopped key exports to Japan in July 2026. The US and China discussed a truce in May 2026, but the restrictions kept biting.
Which Stocks Are Impacted
MP Materials: It runs the Mountain Pass mine and sells NdPr oxide and metal (the main magnet feedstock) plus gadolinium. It also makes magnets in Fort Worth. Second-quarter revenue rose 89% to $108.49 million. Its first heavy rare earth separation circuit remains on track to produce terbium and dysprosium later this year. Management has called yttrium only a potential opportunity. MP has announced no yttrium revenue.
USA Rare Earth: This is the speculative name. Second-quarter revenue was $5.82 million, missing expectations. It owns the Round Top heavy rare earth deposit in Texas, a magnet plant in Stillwater, Oklahoma, and Less Common Metals in the UK. It is also buying Serra Verde for about $2.8 billion. We could not verify any yttrium production.
Energy Fuels: It is mainly a uranium miner. Its White Mesa Mill in Utah produces NdPr oxide and has made high-purity terbium and dysprosium. We could not verify any yttrium production.
Why the Market Shrugged
All three companies are built around magnets, and MP’s chief executive said in August that “the vast majority of demand is no-heavy.” A yttrium shortage hits Japanese aerospace and chip-tool supply chains before it reaches US magnet economics.
The long-term demand case is stronger. Magnets power the motors and actuators in humanoid robots and EVs, as well as data center cooling and power equipment (the same picks-and-shovels angle behind the AI expansion we mapped in a free report on seven suppliers powering AI infrastructure). He added that “30 million or 40 million humanoid robots a year” would use up “100% of rare earth magnet production globally, including China.” New supply from African and friendly projects, however, takes years to reach production and pass customer approval. A shortage measured in months will not wait for it.
Does Japan’s Yttrium Crunch Change the Case for These Stocks?
Not in the near term. The warning shows how much power China holds, but it adds no revenue to any of these three companies. MP remains the only one with revenue at scale and a working heavy rare earth circuit. USA Rare Earth stays a development-stage story.
There are four milestones to watch. First, whether China eases its restrictions on Japan before year-end. Second, whether US yttrium oxide imports resume beyond the 29 tonnes Reuters reported for July. Third, whether MP reports its first dysprosium and terbium output by December 31, 2026. Fourth, whether USA Rare Earth reaches 600 MTPA run-rate capacity at Stillwater in Q4 2026.

Persistent memory chip supply constraints through 2028 fuel outlook
Despite wild swings in the Kospi, brokerages are doubling down on Korean chip stocks, betting the AI-driven memory boom has much further to run.
The benchmark index has seesawed in recent sessions, with chip heavyweights Samsung Electronics and SK hynix at the center of the turbulence as investors reassess the outlook for AI demand.
On Wednesday, the Kospi closed at 5,735.66, up 3.29 percent from the previous session. Samsung and SK hynix each surged more than 7 percent intraday, helping trigger a five-minute buy-side sidecar. Yet analysts remain largely unfazed by the volatility.
In a report Monday, Nomura maintained its bullish outlook for memory chips, forecasting supply bottlenecks through at least 2028 and naming Samsung and SK hynix as its top picks.
The brokerage reiterated its "buy" ratings and price targets of 670,000 won ($505) for Samsung and 4.7 million won for SK hynix — roughly three times and 3.6 times their respective Wednesday closing prices of 223,500 won and 1.294 million won.
Nomura also dismissed market concerns over reports that China's largest DRAM maker, ChangXin Memory Technologies, plans to introduce next-generation server memory by year-end, calling the reaction "excessive."
"The market is underestimating both the breadth of AI demand and the earnings that such strong demand can generate across the value chain," the report said.
"Our investment thesis rests on continued data center deployment and associated memory requirements."
JPMorgan struck a similarly optimistic tone earlier this month, maintaining its "overweight" ratings on Korean and Taiwanese equities. The US investment bank expects AI-related stocks to continue driving Asian market gains next year, extending this year's rally.
JPMorgan also projected tight supply-demand conditions through 2028, saying they would give Asian firms "significant pricing power to go with volume growth," pushing net income across the ecosystem above $1 trillion.
"It remains important to be open-minded about the extent of AI upside," the bank added.
Korean brokerages share that confidence, arguing that sustained AI demand is making the memory industry less vulnerable to traditional boom-and-bust cycles.
"The nature of memory demand in the AI era is different from what it was in the past," said Han Dong-hee, an analyst at SK Securities, in a report Wednesday.
"Memory demand was previously driven by mature industries such as PCs and mobile devices, making it cyclical in nature. But with AI emerging as a new source of demand, the industry's sensitivity to economic cycles has weakened significantly."
Mirae Asset Securities also maintained its "overweight" rating on the semiconductor sector Monday, keeping its price targets unchanged at 400,000 won for Samsung and 3.1 million won for SK hynix.
"We continue to see extremely resilient AI demand, with no signs of a slowdown," said Kim Young-gun, an analyst at Mirae Asset Securities.
"Rather than taking an excessively pessimistic view, investors should place greater confidence in the optimistic outlook offered by leading players."

Hyundai Mobis President Lee Gyu-suk speaks during an Auto Semicon Korea forum, inviting some 90 executives from 53 local chip-related companies, including Samsung Electronics, LX Semicon and SK keyfoundry, on Oct. 21 in Pangyo, Gyeonggi.HYUNDAI MOBIS
PANGYO, Gyeonggi – Hyundai Motor and Kia vehicles will be equipped with Korean-made automotive chips developed by Hyundai Mobis starting in 2029.
With Korea currently relying on imports for more than 95 percent of its automotive chips, Hyundai Mobis is co-developing the chips with domestic semiconductor companies, including Samsung Electronics and SK keyfoundry.
“Starting next year, the chips we have developed will be deployed from the very earliest stages of vehicle testing for Hyundai and Kia,” Hyundai Mobis President Lee Gyu-suk said on Wednesday at Auto Semicon Korea, a forum held in Pangyo, Gyeonggi, for the second year.
“Down the line, we are developing them with sales to overseas automakers in mind,” he added.
The forum, launched last year, brought together 53 companies and institutions to collaborate on developing automotive chips domestically, including Samsung Electronics, SK keyfoundry, Global Technology, ABOV Semiconductor, LX Semicon and Dongwoon Anatech.
Participants in last year’s forum took on about 13 automotive chip projects, nine of which have been confirmed for mass production Hyundai and Kia vehicles.
Since acquiring Hyundai Autron’s semiconductor business in 2020, Hyundai Mobis has expanded its research and development portfolio around two pillars: power semiconductors and system semiconductors.
The urgency dates back to the global chip shortage triggered by the Covid-19 pandemic, when Hyundai Motor’s factories were forced to halt production, leaving thousands of workers idle at home.
Industry Minister Kim Jung-kwan also attended the forum and signed a memorandum of understanding with Hyundai Mobis to establish a research lab in Korea for power semiconductors, a key component in electric vehicles.
The government is building an automotive semiconductor support center in Asan, South Chungcheong, to help verify and evaluate chip reliability. The center is scheduled for completion in 2027.
“We will work actively to build a domestic semiconductor ecosystem robust enough to supply the chips essential to Korea’s auto industry and to play a vital role in its growth,” Lee said.

articles.title: Exclusive: South Korea's 10 Billion Won Satellite K-RadCube Mission Fails - 조선일보
articles.summary: Exclusive: South Korea's 10 Billion Won Satellite K-RadCube Mission Fails  조선일보
articles.full_text:
The South Korean satellite ‘K-RadCube,’ which failed to perform its mission despite an investment of 10 billion Korean won, has been confirmed to have ultimately failed. Launched aboard NASA’s Artemis II in April, the satellite was intended to test the radiation resistance of semiconductors from Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix in space. However, it failed to reach its designated orbit and never established normal communication. The K-RadCube project was led by the government-funded Korea Astronomy and Space Science Institute, with satellite development handled by Nara Space Technology. KT SAT, a subsidiary of KT Group, was responsible for satellite control and ground station operations.
◇Failure Confirmed, But No Plans to Disclose Results
According to the Korea Astronomy and Space Science Institute’s ‘K-RadCube Post-Operation Results Report,’ exclusively obtained by the Chosun Ilbo on the 22nd, K-RadCube repeatedly sent an abnormal response (ACK_MESSAGE_DUPLICATE), meaning “message already received and duplicated,” to all commands from the ground station after separating from the NASA launch vehicle on April 2. Normal communication was never established. The institute concluded that the mission failed to meet the minimum criteria for success, which included “initial orbit insertion” and “collection and transmission of scientific observation data to the ground station.”
Materials submitted to Rep. Choi Hyung-du (People Power Party) of the National Assembly’s Science, ICT, Broadcasting and Communications Committee by the Korea AeroSpace Administration revealed that K-RadCube is estimated to have re-entered Earth’s atmosphere and disintegrated around 8:50 a.m. on April 3. Details about the satellite’s abnormal messages and estimated time of disintegration had not been previously disclosed.
The Korea AeroSpace Administration informed Rep. Choi Hyung-du that “the primary cause was a malfunction in the satellite’s communication system, with a high possibility of hardware failure in the space environment.” The Korea Astronomy and Space Science Institute, which led the mission, ended K-RadCube operations on April 4 and completed the final report in early August.
However, the government had no plans to separately inform the public of the results. In a response submitted to Rep. Choi Hyung-du’s office, the Korea AeroSpace Administration stated, “The research team plans to present the operational results at the American Geophysical Union meeting in December,” adding, “The Korea AeroSpace Administration has no plans for additional announcements.”
◇Full Payment Made Despite Unfulfilled Contract Obligations
Of the 10 billion Korean won budget for K-RadCube, 7.069 billion Korean won was confirmed to have been allocated to Nara Space Technology, the satellite developer. According to materials submitted by the Korea AeroSpace Administration to Rep. Choi Hyung-du, 6.558 billion Korean won has already been paid to the company, with the remaining 511 million Korean won scheduled to be disbursed by the end of the year.
The issue lies in the contract, which included not only satellite manufacturing but also operation and data acquisition. The Korea Astronomy and Space Science Institute stated in its final report, “The transmission of scientific data, specified as a delivery condition in the contract, was also not fulfilled.” This means the contracting agency acknowledged that one of the delivery conditions was not met.
Nonetheless, the institute evaluated, “This result does not necessarily mean that the execution and process of the task were defective.” It judged the tight schedule—developing a cube satellite typically requiring 18–24 months in about a year—and delays in delivering launch-related information as unavoidable constraints.
However, the tight development schedule was a known condition from the project’s inception. The government and the institute proceeded with the project despite these risks and later cited the tight schedule as a major cause of mission failure. This raises questions about the validity of their reasoning. Additionally, paying nearly the full contract amount despite failing to meet delivery conditions is expected to spark controversy.
Rep. Choi Hyung-du stated, “While technical failures can occur in space development projects, paying the full amount despite unmet contractual obligations is a separate issue.” He added, “The Korea AeroSpace Administration and the Korea Astronomy and Space Science Institute must clarify the grounds for deeming the failure unavoidable and the appropriateness of the contract payment.”

articles.title: North Korea: Will Trump-Kim talks happen anytime soon? - DW.com
articles.summary: North Korea: Will Trump-Kim talks happen anytime soon?  DW.com
articles.full_text:
North Korea responded on Thursday to claims by US President Donald Trump that he will be holding talks with leader Kim Jong Un later in the year with a broadside of ballistic missiles.
The South Korean military said Pyongyang launched 10 short-range missiles that landed in the sea off North Korea's east coast.
This came a day after Kim's powerful sister, Kim Yo Jong, said Pyongyang was "completely unaware of" plans for discussions.
Trump's announcement on Wednesday that he is in contact with Kim and that the two leaders would meet later in the year appears to have caught Pyongyang off guard. It comes after the US president said the military would scale back annual military drills with South Korea.
The statement by Kim Yo Jong, director of the Central Committee of the Workers' Party of Korea and one of her brother's closest advisers, dismissed Trump's decision to dramatically scale back the 10-day Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises as "unworthy of comment and [we] have no interest in it at all."
"After Trump's overtures, Kim Yo Jong effectively said downscaling exercises is not enough, and North Korea launched about a dozen missiles in its third firing in two weeks," Leif-Eric Easley, a professor of international studies at Ewha Womans University in Seoul, told DW.
In a statement carried by the state-run Korea Central News Agency (KCNA), Kim Yo Jong mocked South Korea as a "puppet" and indicated that only canceling the drills in their entirety would be seen as a "goodwill measure."
North Korea's position of power
Choo Jae-woo, a professor of foreign policy at South Korea's Kyung Hee University, told DW that unlike in Trump's first term, Pyongyang right now is in a position of power and will likely seek more guarantees before coming to the negotiating table.
"North Korea is not interested in dialogue because Kim was humiliated in 2019 when Trump walked out of their talks in Hanoi," said Choo said.
Those talks ended in acrimony over the US insistence that North would have to scrap its nuclear program.
Pyongyang has since forged a close security and economic alliance with Russia, granting it access to military technology, energy and consumer goods previously beyond its grasp under international sanctions.
"They are in the safe hands of Russia and China and, in the years since Hanoi, Kim has made it his regime's official position that North Korea will never engage in dialogue as long as giving up its nuclear weapons is part of the discussion,” Choo added.
Will Trump-Kim talks happen anytime soon?
Easley said that Pyongyang is unlikely to agree to talks with the US, at least in the immediate future.
"North Korea is practically a combatant in a European war, sending ammunition, missiles and soldiers to Russia as it continues to attack Ukraine," he said.
"Kim is benefiting financially from this illegal trade, incorporating new technologies and battlefield experience into his military and industrial base, and receiving Moscow's blessing for de facto nuclear status."
That, in turn, gives Kim leverage to demand greater support from Beijing. Pyongyang is also aware that time is not on Trump's side.
Trump has not yet publicly confirmed a date and venue for talks with Kim, and no agenda has been presented, casting doubt on whether a meeting will take place. The upcoming US midterm elections on November 3 add more political urgency to Trump's timeline.
On the other hand, the North Korean leader may sense that this may be his best opportunity to strike some sort of deal with the US while Trump is still in office.
In her statement earlier this week, Kim Yo Jong said the relationship between Trump and her brother is "still excellent."
Seoul welcomes progress
And while the South Korean government has broadly welcomed Trump's claim that he will meet with Kim later in the year and reiterated that it no longer considers denuclearization of the North a prerequisite for talks, there are concerns among ordinary people in the South, Choo said.
"The fear is that Trump will simply ignore South Korea's security needs and deal directly with North Korea because he is so desperate to get an agreement signed," he said.
"There needs to be close coordination between Seoul and Washington on what is being discussed and agreed because any agreements that are made will affect us far more than the US," he said.
Media reports suggest that the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum on November 18 and 19 in the Chinese city of Shenzhen could provide a suitable venue for Trump and Kim to meet in person.
Edited by: Wesley Rahn

Abstract
According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Semiconductor Diffusion Equipment market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture.
The global semiconductor diffusion equipment market is entering a structurally significant phase as chipmakers ramp investments in leading-edge logic and memory capacity. Diffusion equipment, which includes batch furnaces and related systems for dopant introduction and thermal processing, sits on the critical path of every wafer fab. Demand is being pulled forward by the transition to sub-3nm gate-all-around logic and 200-plus-layer 3D NAND, where precise thermal budgets and contamination control become non-negotiable.
At the same time, national semiconductor self-sufficiency programs across the US, Europe, Japan, and India are creating new fab clusters, each requiring localized qualification and support infrastructure. The supply landscape remains concentrated among a handful of global OEMs, protected by deep process integration IP and high switching costs. Pricing power is shifting toward service and upgrades, with recurring revenue streams often exceeding initial tool cost.
This report provides a structured, commercially grounded analysis of the market from 2026 to 2035, covering demand drivers, end-use sectors, regional dynamics, competitive positioning, and the qualification burden that shapes supplier selection. It is designed for equipment manufacturers, subsystem suppliers, investors, and strategic entrants seeking a clear view of where value pools are forming and how procurement logic is evolving.
The baseline scenario for the global semiconductor diffusion equipment market points to steady expansion through 2035, supported by the inexorable push toward advanced process nodes and the geographic diversification of fab capacity. The market is expected to register a CAGR of approximately 6.5% over the forecast period, with the market index rising from 100 in 2025 to around 185 by 2035. This growth is not linear; it will be punctuated by capex cycles tied to leading-edge foundry and memory investments, but the underlying trajectory remains positive.
The strongest demand pull comes from the transition to gate-all-around logic at 3nm and below, and from 3D NAND stacks exceeding 200 layers, both of which require tighter thermal budget control and higher equipment performance. Diffusion equipment demand is also being supported by the build-out of new fabs in the United States, Europe, Japan, and India, driven by government incentives. However, these new facilities will require extensive qualification cycles, delaying revenue recognition. The aftermarket for refurbished and legacy-node equipment provides a stable counter-cyclical buffer, particularly for automotive and industrial semiconductors.
Supply remains concentrated, with fewer than ten global players controlling the majority of system-level design-ins. Pricing power is concentrated in the service and upgrade layer, where proprietary consumables and process know-how create recurring revenue. Risks include geopolitical export controls, which could fragment the market further, and the potential for a capex digestion phase after the current investment wave. Overall, the outlook is cautiously optimistic, with growth driven by technology transitions and geographic expansion rather than unit-volume increases alone.

Primary Demand Drivers
- Transition to advanced nodes (sub-3nm gate-all-around logic and 200+ layer 3D NAND) requiring tighter thermal budget control and higher equipment performance
- Geographic diversification of semiconductor manufacturing driven by national self-sufficiency policies, creating new fab clusters and parallel qualification pathways
- Rising demand for mature-node semiconductors in automotive, industrial, and IoT applications, sustaining demand for refurbished and legacy diffusion equipment
- Increasing complexity of device architectures, including 3D structures and new materials, which raises the number of diffusion steps per wafer
- Growth in memory capacity investments, particularly DRAM and 3D NAND, as data center and AI workloads drive bit demand
- Government incentives and subsidies for domestic semiconductor production in the US, EU, Japan, and India, accelerating fab construction and equipment orders
Potential Growth Constraints
- High qualification burden and long design-in cycles for new equipment, which slow supplier diversification and delay revenue from new fabs
- Geopolitical export controls and trade restrictions that fragment the market and limit access to certain regions and customers
- Cyclicality of semiconductor capex, with potential digestion phases after periods of heavy investment leading to temporary demand declines
- Technical complexity and high R&D costs required to keep pace with advanced node requirements, posing barriers for smaller suppliers
- Supply chain constraints for critical components such as high-purity quartz and specialty ceramics, which can extend lead times and increase costs

Semiconductor Foundry (estimated share: 45%)
The foundry segment represents the largest and most technologically demanding end-use sector for semiconductor diffusion equipment. Foundries are ramping production at 5nm, 3nm, and below, where gate-all-around transistor architectures require precise dopant placement and ultra-low contamination levels. Diffusion furnaces are used for well formation, source/drain doping, and thermal annealing steps, with each advanced node adding process steps and tighter specifications. The demand story here is driven by capacity expansions at leading foundries such as TSMC, Samsung Foundry, and Intel Foundry, as well as the emergence of new foundries in the US, Europe, and Japan.

This segment is expected to grow at a CAGR above the market average, supported by the relentless pursuit of Moore's Law and the increasing complexity of logic chips for AI, mobile, and high-performance computing applications. DRAM scaling, meanwhile, requires precise dopant control for buried wordlines and capacitor structures. articles.title: What to make of China, North Korea's new cross-border bridge - upi
articles.summary: What to make of China, North Korea's new cross-border bridge  upi
articles.full_text:
Oct. 22 (UPI) -- Chinese and North Korean officials last week celebrated the opening of the New Yalu River Bridge, a long-delayed crossing between Dandong and Sinuiju that could become the primary route for road traffic between the long-standing allies.
While the bridge is a milestone in Sino-North Korean relations practically and symbolically, its opening offers deeper insights into the Kim Jong Un regime's foreign policy designs.
In particular, the timing of the opening, when considered alongside a similar bridge opening with Russia, offers clues to North Korea's current prioritization of relations with its two major partners.
Long-dormant bridge
The "new" Yalu River Bridge is somewhat of a misnomer. Construction finished in 2014, but the roadway remained mostly unused for the next 12 years. Beijing and Pyongyang signed an agreement to construct the cross-border bridge in February 2010, downstream from their original road-and-rail crossing.
Construction followed soon thereafter, continuing even after Kim Jong Il's death and Kim Jong Un's succession in 2011.
There has never been an official statement from either government as to why the bridge remained closed after its completion. There are two important reasons, however, why North Korea may have suspended the cooperative project.
First, Beijing supported U.N. sanctions targeting North Korea's nuclear and missile programs. While the Kim Jong Il regime had tolerated China's role in passing U.N. Security Council Resolution 1718 (2006) and 1874 (2009), Kim Jong Un had different ambitions from his father in his pursuit of a viable nuclear arsenal.
Beijing's cooperation with international denuclearization efforts were incongruent with the Kim Jong Un regime's byungjin policy, which sought to advance the nuclear weapons development alongside economic growth.
Second, and perhaps more importantly, the bridge project was closely associated with Kim Jong Un's uncle, Jang Song Thaek. Jang was a key interlocutor between Beijing and Pyongyang and a chief proponent for the Hwanggumphyong and Wihwa Islands Economic Zone.
The New Yalu River Bridge was set to serve as the primary transit point for what would have been North Korea's second special economic zone, complementing the Rason SEZ along the country's borders with Russia and China.
Jang's ties to Beijing, however, ultimately became a liability. Amid suspicions of disloyalty and fears that China might plot to supplant Kim Jong Un with his uncle, the North Korean government dragged Jang out of a party meeting in December 2013, tried him for crimes against the state and executed him.
The purge of Jang Song Thaek extended beyond his execution to an effort to erase his legacy. The North Korean government removed records of Jang from state media and history, while also leading to the abandonment of Jang's China-focused projects.
The bridge's prolonged inactivity, therefore, may have reflected the political fallout from Jang's purge, given its association with his China-focused political and economic agenda.
Symbolic reset with China
Given the complicated history and long delay, the opening of the bridge carries both practical and symbolic significance.
In practice, it opens another artery for cargo shipments between China and North Korea. Chinese media outlets have touted the bridge as being able to handle crossings of up to 20,000 vehicles and 50,000 people daily.
Given the existing capacity for maritime shipping and the fact that the two countries are unlikely to max out cross-border transit anytime soon, this is not a gamechanger, but it is a meaningful improvement over the previous bridge capacity.
Symbolically, the bridge opening is important, as it signals to Beijing that the two governments have overcome previous obstacles in the Sino-North Korea relationship. After giving Beijing the cold shoulder the past few years, the Kim regime is moving forward with its post-COVID-19 reset, which began in earnest with the Xi Jinping-Kim Jong Un summit in Pyongyang in June.
Several working-level engagements have followed the leader-level meeting, and this bridge opening is a tangible outcome of those efforts. The key question now is with an improved cross-border roadway in place, how do the two countries intend to use it?
Tale of two bridges
The New Yalu River Bridge was not the only cross-border bridge opened this fall Last month, Russian and North Korean officials inaugurated the Tumangang-Khasan bridge, also known as the Yakov Novichenko Bridge.
This is a first-of-its-kind cross-border roadway, and while Russia and the DPRK had long maintained a rail connection through Khasan, this bridge offers another option for transit besides rail and sea.
The opening of the bridge was postponed on the Russian side based on failed contract performance. Reporting from inside North Korea suggests that the delay frustrated North Korean officials for the project, who had been prepared to open it earlier.
Despite the delays, the Russia-North Korea bridge still opened first, and the sequence of the ceremonies, the seniority of the delegations and the names chosen for the bridges offer important indicators for North Korea's diplomatic preferences.
It is notable that the North Korean government waited until after the opening of the Russo-North Korean bridge before opening the bridge with China.
Deliberate prioritizing
Since the New Yalu River Bridge was already constructed, Pyongyang could have elected to move forward with the opening any time after the Kim-Xi summit in June. However, the sequencing raises the possibility that the Kim regime deliberately prioritized the Russian crossing.
Additionally, the composition of in-person delegations suggests a difference in political emphasis.
Vice-Premier Kim Tok Hun, a longtime member of Kim Jong Un's inner circle, was the lead delegate for the Russia-North Korea bridge opening. At the New Yalu River Bridge event, the senior North Korean official was Yang Myong Chol, the regional chief secretary of the Workers' Party of Korea's North Pyongan Provincial Committee.
The difference in seniority is notable given the practical and symbolic importance North Korea attaches to political protocol.
Finally, the names chosen for the bridges carry weight. Moscow and Pyongyang used the name Yakov Novichenko for their new crossing, invoking a historical figure associated with North Korea's first leader, Kim Il Sung. In the official Russian and North Korean narrative, Novichenko is remembered for saving Kim Il Sung during an assassination attempt in 1946.
By contrast, China calls its recently opened crossing the New Yalu River Bridge, while North Korea uses the Korean name, the Amnok River Bridge. Whether due to a disagreement over nomenclature or a deliberate choice to stick with respective naming conventions, the two sides did not adopt a common name.
Taken together, these differences are important indicators about the prioritization of North Korea's external relationships. They signal that while Beijing and Pyongyang are once again deepening ties, the Kim regime is likely making choices that privileges Moscow. How long this will continue is important to observe.
Going forward, traffic across the bridges will offer a practical measure of how North Korea's relationships with China and Russia are evolving. The volume and composition of cross-border traffic, along with the activities necessitating cross-border transit that Pyongyang chooses to publicize, are useful indicators as to how Pyongyang is moving forward in its foreign policy designs.
Undoubtedly, the New Yalu River Bridge remains an important milestone in the Sino-North Korean relationship. The circumstances of its opening, however, suggest that Beijing is not yet gaining ground on Moscow in Pyongyang's strategic calculations.

① The Bank of Korea kept its benchmark interest rate unchanged at 3.00% while raising its forecast for domestic economic growth; ② The semiconductor cycle remains robust, and as the growth dividend spreads to other sectors, South Korea's economy is expected to sustain a high‑growth trajectory; ③ Strong semiconductor exports will help maintain a sizable current‑account surplus, with the surplus projected to exceed earlier expectations.
Cailian Press, October 22 (Editor Liu Rui): On October 22 local time, the Bank of Korea released its October monetary policy statement, keeping the benchmark interest rate unchanged at 3.00%, in line with market expectations. Earlier, the bank had raised rates twice in a row, in July and August.
Meanwhile, the Bank of Korea has also revised upward its economic growth forecast, projecting that GDP growth this year and next will "rise significantly" compared with the projections released in August.
As a major chip-producing country, the Bank of Korea highlighted in its economic report the sector's positive impact on the national economy. The bank forecasts that the semiconductor upcycle will persist, with Governor Lee Ju-yeol projecting that chip prices could rise further in the future.
The semiconductor industry's cyclical momentum remains robust.
According to a report by the Bank of Korea, despite external uncertainties stemming from geopolitical risks in the Middle East, the semiconductor cycle remains robust. As the growth dividends of the semiconductor sector spill over into other industries, South Korea's economy is expected to sustain a high‑growth trajectory.
Benefiting from the continued ramp-up in AI infrastructure investments by global cloud giants, South Korea's leading semiconductor firms have seen a surge in performance: Samsung Electronics posted quarterly operating profit of KRW 107.4 trillion in the third quarter of this year, becoming the first private company worldwide to exceed KRW 100 trillion in quarterly operating profit; SK Hynix has yet to release its earnings report, but brokerage firms generally expect its third-quarter operating profit to surpass KRW 80 trillion.
Despite the recent sharp volatility in South Korean chip stocks, the Bank of Korea does not appear overly concerned. The central bank stated that the heightened price swings reflect market anxieties over a slowdown in AI-related investment, while the steep declines stem from worries about a deceleration in the semiconductor industry's profitability.
Bank of Korea Governor Lee Ju-yeol stated that, compared with chipmakers' stock prices, it is more prudent to focus on chip prices. He expects that, with no signs of a decline, chip prices could continue to rise.
On the outlook for economic growth, the Bank of Korea had previously projected 3.3% this year and 2.9% next year. On Thursday, the bank did not release a new, more precise growth forecast, but it did confirm that this year's expansion will be "significantly higher" than its earlier projection. Meanwhile, South Korea's Ministry of Economy and Finance has estimated that economic growth could reach as high as 3.6% this year.
Looking ahead to next year, the central bank expects the semiconductor upcycle to persist, with the sector's economic weight continuing to rise and its spillover effects spreading further, keeping South Korea's economic growth at a robust level. At the same time, developments in the Middle East, trends in AI‑related capital spending and the trajectory of the semiconductor cycle, as well as fluctuations in domestic and global financial conditions, will all constitute key sources of uncertainty shaping South Korea's economic outlook.
Strong demand for semiconductors will support South Korea's trade surplus.
On the inflation front, the Bank of Korea has warned that, with cost pressures continuing to be passed on and demand‑side price‑increase pressures gradually intensifying, South Korea's CPI inflation rate is likely to remain above the 2% policy target for an extended period. For this year, both overall CPI and core inflation are broadly in line with the August projections, at 2.7% and 2.5%, respectively; meanwhile, next year's inflation indicators are expected to exceed earlier forecasts, which had projected CPI at 2.3% and core inflation at 2.5%.
In the third quarter of this year, both South Korea's CPI and core CPI rose 2.9% year on year. Sharp fluctuations in international oil prices, mounting upward pressure on domestic demand, the depreciation of the Korean won against the U.S. dollar, and the government's price-stabilization policies together constitute two-way risks to South Korea's inflation.
On the trade and employment fronts, robust semiconductor exports are expected to keep South Korea's current-account surplus at a high level, with the surplus projected to exceed earlier expectations; meanwhile, the number of new jobs created and the employment rate are broadly in line with previous forecasts.

articles.title: Japan government, BOJ gap on inflation laid bare ahead of key policy meeting - The Standard (HK)
articles.summary: Japan government, BOJ gap on inflation laid bare ahead of key policy meeting  The Standard (HK)
articles.full_text:
Japan has yet to meet the conditions for officially declaring victory over deflation, Economy Minister Minoru Kiuchi said on Friday, exposing a divide with the Bank of Japan as it sees the economy on the cusp of durably achieving its 2 percent inflation goal.
Kiuchi's remarks, from a close ally of dovish Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, underscore a disconnect between the government and the BOJ on price moves.
They also come ahead of the BOJ's policy meeting next week, when it is seen signalling that underlying inflation has hit its 2 percent target as the Iran war-induced energy shock and rising import costs from a weak yen push up prices.
The government, however, has stopped short of declaring victory over deflation, saying it needs clearer evidence that the economy will not slide back into a period of persistent price declines.
"We need to be cautious in making the decision and look comprehensively at consumer price moves, GDP deflator and factors driving underlying inflation," Kiuchi said when asked whether the government could formally declare an end to deflation.
"It's important that Japan does not revert to deflation," he said, adding it was premature to declare an end to deflation.
Kiuchi made the remarks at a news conference, when asked how the government will align its view on deflation with the BOJ's assessment that underlying inflation may have hit its target.
While fuel subsidies have helped temper price pressures, core consumer inflation has hovered near the BOJ's 2 percent target for four years, challenging the government's view that Japan has yet to fully escape deflation.
The core consumer price index (CPI), which excludes volatile fresh food but includes fuel costs, rose 2.1 percent in September from a year earlier, data showed on Friday.
Some analysts say the government's reluctance to declare an end to deflation reflects concern that doing so would narrow its room to pursue accommodative fiscal and monetary policy.
Declaring an official end to deflation could also draw calls to tweak a joint government-BOJ statement, signed in 2013, pledging coordinated efforts by the two sides to end deflation including by "pursuing monetary easing to achieve the BOJ's inflation target at the earliest date possible." The government and BOJ reaffirmed the joint statement in 2025.
"I hope the BOJ conducts monetary policy appropriately to stably and sustainably achieve its 2 percent inflation target, taking into account the principles of the joint BOJ-government statement," Kiuchi said.
Considered an advocate of loose monetary policy, Kiuchi has repeatedly signaled his reservation over the BOJ's rate-hike plans.
Kiuchi said on Tuesday he hoped to attend the central bank's policy meeting next week, when it is seen keeping interest rates steady, but revising up its inflation forecast and signalling its resolve to keep hiking borrowing costs.

articles.title: Australia hits North Korean 'shadow bankers' with fresh sanctions - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
articles.summary: Australia hits North Korean 'shadow bankers' with fresh sanctions  ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation

source_detail.name: ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation

articles.full_text:
In short:
North Korean companies have been accused of employing workers to launder billions of dollars through cybercrime.
Foreign Minister Penny Wong has announced fresh sanctions and says the "export of labour" violates UN sanctions.
What's next?
Australia continues to call on North Korea to comply with its international obligations.
The federal government has hit two North Korean companies and "shadow bankers" with sanctions for employing fraudulent online workers who help Pyongyang evade UN sanctions and earn cash for its nuclear weapons program.
The US and several other nations have accused North Korea of setting up an international network of IT workers to launder billions of dollars through cybercrime and overseas earnings.
The two men sanctioned by Australia — Sim Hyon Sop and Yu Py Ung — have been identified by US authorities as key financial brokers for the regime.
In 2024 the US Treasury called Yu Pu Ung "a linchpin in the DPRK's illicit financial activities [who] is skilled at employing various schemes to avoid detection".
The year before that the FBI offered a $5 million dollar reward for information to assist with the capture of Sim Hyon Sop, who the agency said helped North Korea evade sanctions.
He "allegedly played a pivotal role in defrauding U.S. banks by remitting U.S. dollar payments to facilitate trade on behalf of North Korea," the FBI said.
Foreign Minister Penny Wong said the sanctioned companies employed North Koreans who impersonated nationals from other countries, worked on online platforms and sent their income to key North Korean government agencies.
Senator Wong said that was "a violation of UN Security Council resolutions that prohibit North Korea's export of labour" and that Australia was acting "in coordination with international partners, including the European Union".
"Australian sanctions reinforce our ongoing efforts, alongside international partners, to disrupt North Korea's illicit revenue-generating networks and increase pressure on the regime to comply with its international obligations and abandon its nuclear and ballistic missile programs," she said.
North Korea has repeatedly denied setting up shadow financial networks and says the allegations against it are fabricated.
But law enforcement and financial institutions from across the world say there is a mountain of evidence to back their accusations.
In July the US, Australia, Japan, South Korea, the UK, Canada and several European nations warned that North Korean workers were employing "increasingly sophisticated methods, including the integration of AI, to obfuscate their identities and expand their activities globally".
They urged countries around the world to "deepen their understanding of North Korean IT worker schemes and implement measures to counter [them]".
New Zealand's cyber authorities also warned in advisory earlier this year that a North Korean operative posing as remote contractor was unwittingly hired by a local business.
Senator Wong said Australia continued to call on North Korea to "comply fully with UN Security Council resolutions and to take concrete steps towards complete, verifiable and irreversible denuclearisation".
